performers: Reinald Werrenrath, baritone; Mabel Garrison, soprano; orchestra conducted by Josef Pasternack
question: When the two voices finally move together, what has changed musically—and what remains unresolved dramatically?
intro: On this acoustic Victor disc, Don Giovanni’s invitation and Zerlina’s hesitation begin as separate phrases and move towards a shared dance. Reinald Werrenrath and Mabel Garrison sing the roles, with Josef Pasternack conducting.

sections.label: Invitation and hesitation
sections.mNote: Separate phrases in the score’s A-major Andante

sections.label: The exchange tightens
sections.mNote: Shorter replies move towards a shared decision

sections.label: Together · Allegro
sections.mNote: A quicker 6/8 dance replaces the opening metre

cues.title: An invitation gets an answer
cues.text: Don Giovanni offers a smoothly shaped invitation. Zerlina answers in a related musical language, but her words hesitate. Listen for the difference between borrowing someone’s melody and agreeing with what that person proposes.
cues.evidence: Schirmer Italian–English vocal score, plate 15147, No. 7, printed pp. 64–65 (PDF pp. 78–79): successive solo phrases. Report has moderate relative level across 0:00–0:40. No exact word onset is assigned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written for Prague
cues.text: Don Giovanni belongs to Mozart’s Prague opera of 1787, with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. This duet is one encounter inside a much larger drama, not a self-contained portrait of an uncomplicated romance.
cues.evidence: Mozart composer biography; Don Giovanni work catalogue and Schirmer vocal score, Act I, No. 7.

cues.title: The answer resembles the offer
cues.text: Zerlina’s reply resembles the phrase she has just heard, but her text says that she would—and would not—go. Listen for how a shared melodic shape can carry different intentions in the two voices.
cues.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, printed pp. 64–65: Don Giovanni’s “Là ci darem la mano” and Zerlina’s “Vorrei, e non vorrei”. Report boundaries 0:52 and 0:56 support the changing vocal span; no syllable is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One side of a Victor disc
cues.text: This performance is recorded in Camden on 18 February 1920. The issued master is take 2 of matrix B-23741, released as the single-faced Victor 87569; the disc is not evidence for an entire opera performance.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress National Jukebox jukebox-35668; DAHR matrix B-23741 and disc object 55816. These catalogues establish session, take and carrier, independently of the Internet Archive mirror.

cues.title: A recurring collaboration
cues.text: Da Ponte also supplies the librettos for The Marriage of Figaro and Così fan tutte. In these collaborations, an ensemble can make characters share musical time without making their motives identical.
cues.evidence: Mozart composer biography, operas of 1786, 1787 and 1790; the final sentence is a listening proposition, not a biographical claim about the performers.

cues.title: Two voices share a dance
cues.text: The Allegro changes to 6/8, and the two characters sing together in parallel phrases. The separate exchange becomes a shared movement forward; listen for the new rhythmic grouping as well as the combined voices.
cues.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, printed pp. 66–67 (PDF pp. 80–81), Allegro 6/8 “Andiam, andiam, mio bene”; report strongest boundary 2:22 and lower spectral brightness from the 2:25 window. Marker 2:22 is provisional, not a lyric alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A duet, not a resolution
cues.text: The closing phrases make the voices fit together and bring the number to a firm cadence. In the opera, however, the story continues immediately. Musical agreement at the end of this disc is not the same thing as a settled dramatic situation.
cues.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, printed pp. 67–68 (PDF pp. 81–82): repeated joint phrases, A-major close, then Donna Elvira’s recitative. Report falls from a stronger 3:00 window towards the 3:11.97 endpoint.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Long phrases become closer replies
transitions.how: The two opening statements establish a shared melodic vocabulary. As the exchange continues, shorter replies bring the voices closer together in the musical conversation. The A-major framework remains recognisable; changing phrase lengths and the relation between the voices carry the dramatic pressure.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, printed pp. 64–66; report boundary 1:18 supports a broad shift within the vocal dialogue. The marker does not claim an exact word or a verified acoustic-disc cut.

transitions.title: The dialogue becomes a joint dance
transitions.how: Hesitant, separated gestures give way to the shared “Andiam” passage. Mozart changes from the Andante’s 2/4 to an Allegro in 6/8, and the two voices move together. A new metre and texture make the change unmistakable without requiring a new home key.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, printed p. 66, Allegro after the paused dialogue; report strongest novelty boundary at 2:22 and a sustained spectral change from 2:25. The score establishes the metre change, not the automated tempo or key estimator.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
